quals-wisconsin-algebra-1998s-01.title: Sylow in the normal subgroup
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1998s-01.body:
**(i)** Since $N\trianglelefteq G$, $P\cap N$ and $Q\cap N$ are Sylow $p$-subgroups of $N$. By Sylow's theorem in $N$, $Q\cap N=(P\cap N)^n$ for some $n\in N$. Because $p$ divides $|N|$, $Q\cap N\neq1$. Now $Q\supseteq Q\cap N$ and $P^n\supseteq(P\cap N)^n=Q\cap N$, and $P^n$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$. By uniqueness of the Sylow $p$-subgroup containing $Q\cap N$, $Q=P^n$.

**(ii)** Let $\bar{\ }\colon G\to G/N$. Every Sylow $p$-subgroup of $\bar G$ is the image $\bar P$ of some $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$. Given two, $\bar P$ and $\bar Q$, (i) gives $Q=P^n$ with $n\in N$, so $\bar Q=\bar P^{\bar n}=\bar P$ since $\bar n=1$. So $G/N$ has a unique Sylow $p$-subgroup. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1998s-02.body:

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1998s-03.title: Kummer-type towers
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1998s-03.body:
Work in a fixed algebraic closure of $K$; let $\zeta\in F$ be a primitive $p$th root of unity.

**(i)** Let $f=x^p-a$ and let $E$ be its splitting field over $K$. If $a=0$, $E=K$. Otherwise, if $\beta$ is any root, the roots of $f$ are $\zeta^i\beta$ ($0\le i<p$), so $K[\beta]=E$. Factor $f=g_1\cdots g_r$ into irreducibles in $K[x]$, and let $\beta_j$ be a root of $g_j$. Then $\deg g_j=|K[\beta_j]:K|=|E:K|$ for every $j$, so $p=\deg f=r\,|E:K|$. As $p$ is prime, $|E:K|\in\{1,p\}$. Clearly $E$ contains a $p$th root of $a$.

**(ii)** Let $K$ be the splitting field over $F$ of some $g\in F[x]$, and let $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)=\{\sigma_1=1,\sigma_2,\dots,\sigma_n\}$. Put $h(x)=\prod_{i=1}^n(x^p-\sigma_i(a))$. Its coefficients are fixed by $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$ (which permutes the factors), so $h\in F[x]$. Let $E$ be the splitting field of $gh$ over $F$; it contains $K$ and a $p$th root of $a$, and $E/F$ is Galois (a splitting field in characteristic $0$).

For $0\le j\le n$ let $E_j$ be the field generated over $K$ by the roots of $\prod_{i\le j}(x^p-\sigma_i(a))$, so $K=E_0\subseteq E_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq E_n=E$. $E_j$ is the splitting field of $x^p-\sigma_j(a)$ over $E_{j-1}$, and $F\subseteq E_{j-1}$ contains $\zeta$, so by (i) $|E_j:E_{j-1}|\in\{1,p\}$. Therefore $|E:K|=\prod_j|E_j:E_{j-1}|$ is a power of $p$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1998s-04.title: Cayley–Hamilton and induction
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1998s-04.body:
Let $n=\dim V$.

**(i)** Let $\chi(x)=x^n+a_1x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{n-1}x+a_n$ be the characteristic polynomial. By Cayley–Hamilton, $0=T^n+a_1T^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{n-1}T+a_nI$. Taking traces (trace is linear) and using $\mathrm{tr}\,T^k=0$ for $k\ge1$, we get $0=a_n\,\mathrm{tr}\,I=na_n$. In characteristic $0$, $n\neq0$ (for $n\ge1$), so $a_n=0$. Since $\det T=\pm a_n=0$, $T$ is singular, hence not surjective: $T(V)\ne V$.

**(ii)** $T(T(V))\subseteq T(V)$, so $S$ is well defined. Choose a basis of $T(V)$ and extend it to a basis of $V$. Since $T$ maps $V$ into $T(V)$, its matrix (columns = images) is $B=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, where $A$ is the matrix of $S$. Then $B^k=\begin{pmatrix}A^k&A^{k-1}C\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, so $\mathrm{tr}\,S^k=\mathrm{tr}\,A^k=\mathrm{tr}\,B^k=\mathrm{tr}\,T^k=0$.

**(iii)** Induct on $n$; for $n=0$ there is nothing to prove. For $n\ge1$, $\dim T(V)<n$ by (i), and $S$ satisfies the hypothesis by (ii), so $S$ is nilpotent by induction: $S^j=0$ for some $j$. Then $T^{j+1}(V)=T^j(T(V))=S^j(T(V))=0$, so $T$ is nilpotent. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1998s-05.title: Induction on the nilpotency exponent
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1998s-05.body:
**(i)** Let $H=\ker\theta^2$. Then $\theta(H)\subseteq\ker\theta$, and the restriction $\theta|_H\colon H\to\ker\theta$ has kernel $H\cap\ker\theta=\ker\theta$. So $|H|=|\theta(H)|\cdot|\ker\theta|\le|\ker\theta|^2<\infty$.

Now show $G$ finite by induction on $n$. If $n=1$, $\theta(G)=1$, so $G=\ker\theta$ is finite. For $n\ge2$, let $K=\ker\theta\trianglelefteq G$. Since $\theta(K)=1\subseteq K$, $\theta$ induces a homomorphism $\varphi\colon G/K\to G/K$, $gK\mapsto\theta(g)K$. Its kernel is $\{gK:\theta(g)\in K\}=\ker\theta^2/K$, which is finite by the above. Also $\varphi^{n-1}(G/K)=\theta^{n-1}(G)K/K=K/K$ is trivial, because $\theta(\theta^{n-1}(G))=\theta^n(G)=1$ gives $\theta^{n-1}(G)\subseteq K$. By induction $G/K$ is finite, and $K$ is finite, so $G$ is finite.

**(ii)** $\theta\colon G\to\theta(G)$ is surjective and maps $\theta(G)$ onto $\theta^2(G)$, so it maps each coset $x\theta(G)$ onto the coset $\theta(x)\theta^2(G)$; hence $|\theta(G):\theta^2(G)|\le|G:\theta(G)|$ and $|G:\theta^2(G)|=|G:\theta(G)|\,|\theta(G):\theta^2(G)|<\infty$.

Induct on $n$. If $n=1$, $\theta(G)=1$ has finite index, so $G$ is finite. For $n\ge2$, let $\varphi=\theta|_{\theta(G)}\colon\theta(G)\to\theta(G)$. Then $\varphi^{n-1}(\theta(G))=\theta^n(G)=1$ and $|\theta(G):\varphi(\theta(G))|=|\theta(G):\theta^2(G)|<\infty$. By induction $\theta(G)$ is finite, and since it has finite index, $G$ is finite. ∎
